posts.title: Mixture of Experts: Scaling Params Without Scaling Compute
posts.subtitle: Why DeepSeek-V3 has 671B parameters but only touches 37B of them per token
posts.summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) replaces a transformer's single feed-forward block with many smaller 'expert' blocks and a learned router that activates only a handful per token. That decouples a model's total parameter capacity from its per-token compute cost — which is why DeepSeek-V3 can carry 671B parameters while only computing with 37B of them for any given token. The catch: you still have to store and shard every expert, and keeping the router from collapsing onto a favorite few takes real engineering.

slides.title: Mixture of Experts: Scaling Params Without Scaling Compute
slides.body: MoE swaps one big feed-forward block per transformer layer for many smaller 'expert' blocks and a router that activates only a few per token — so a model can carry far more total parameters while each token's forward pass stays cheap.
bullets: Traces to Shazeer et al.'s 2017 'Outrageously Large Neural Networks', scaled into transformers by Google's GShard (2020) and Switch Transformer (2021)
Mixtral 8x7B: 46.7B total params, ~12.9B active per token (top-2 of 8 experts)
DeepSeek-V3: 671B total params, 37B active per token (top-8 of 256 experts)

slides.title: Dense models pay full price for every token
slides.body: In a standard (dense) transformer, every parameter in every feed-forward layer runs for every token, whether or not that token needed it.
bullets: A 70B dense model spends all 70B parameters' worth of compute on 'the' and on a multi-step proof alike — no specialization, no skipping
Scaling a dense model from 70B to 700B multiplies both training AND inference compute by roughly 10x, which quickly becomes impractical
Capacity (total parameters) and compute (FLOPs per token) don't have to be the same knob — that's the gap MoE exploits

slides.title: A learned router picks which experts fire
slides.body: Each MoE layer replaces one FFN with N parallel 'expert' FFNs of identical shape but independent weights, plus a small router network.
bullets: The router is a linear layer + softmax over N experts, run per token, producing a score for each expert
Only the top-k highest-scoring experts actually run for that token — the rest are skipped entirely, not just down-weighted
The chosen experts' outputs are combined via a weighted sum (using the router's own scores) and added back into the residual stream, just like a normal FFN output

slides.title: Load balancing is the part that actually breaks
slides.body: Nothing in the basic setup stops the router from collapsing onto a favorite handful of experts, wasting the rest as dead weight.
bullets: Unchecked training reinforces early-popular experts ('rich get richer'), leaving many experts undertrained
Switch Transformer and successors add an auxiliary load-balancing loss that penalizes uneven routing, nudging tokens toward underused experts

DeepSeek-V3 instead uses an auxiliary-loss-free scheme: a per-expert bias that's adjusted each step based on how overloaded or underloaded that expert currently is, avoiding the accuracy tax a balancing loss imposes on the main objective
Imbalance also hurts hardware: experts are usually sharded across GPUs, so a lopsided router leaves some GPUs idle while others queue up all-to-all traffic

slides.title: Worked example: DeepSeek-V3's 671B-but-37B trick
slides.body: DeepSeek-V3 splits 671B total parameters across 256 routed experts (plus a shared expert) per MoE layer, but activates only 37B per token.
bullets: One forward pass for one token touches: the always-on shared expert + its top-8 routed experts out of 256 — about 3% of the routed-expert pool, per layer
That's why DeepSeek-V3's reported training compute (~2.788M H800 GPU-hours) looks closer to a ~37B dense model than a 671B one
But the weights for all 671B parameters still have to live somewhere: MoE saves compute per token, not VRAM — serving it well means spreading experts across many GPUs/nodes

slides.title: Dense vs. MoE, concretely

rows: Needs expert parallelism, load balancing, all-to-all comms

slides.title: The tradeoffs that keep MoE from being free lunch
slides.body: The sparsity that saves compute doesn't save memory, and it adds real systems complexity.
bullets: Low-batch, single-user serving loses much of the benefit: you still pay to load every expert's weights, and a small batch may not even fill one expert efficiently
Fine-tuning is trickier — a handful of experts can overfit on a narrow dataset while others go untouched, so updates need care about which layers change
Cross-GPU token dispatch (all-to-all) can dominate wall-clock time on slow interconnects — MoE's compute savings assume fast NVLink/InfiniBand networking
Below a modest parameter count, the routing and balancing machinery often isn't worth it — a simple dense model is easier to train and serve and can be just as good

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.body: MoE isn't a different model family — it's a way to buy capacity without buying proportional compute.
bullets: A learned router + top-k selection lets a token activate only a handful of experts, decoupling total parameter count from per-token compute cost
Load balancing (an auxiliary loss, or DeepSeek-V3's bias-based scheme) is what keeps every expert actually useful instead of a few absorbing all the training signal
The trade is memory and communication, not compute: every expert's weights must still be stored and shardable, since any token could route to any of them
This is why most open frontier models since 2024 (Mixtral, DeepSeek-V3, and others) lean on some MoE variant instead of scaling a dense model further

questions.prompt: What problem does Mixture-of-Experts primarily solve?
options: It removes the need for a router entirely
It decouples a model's total parameter capacity from the compute cost of processing each token
It eliminates backpropagation during training
It converts a transformer into a convolutional network
questions.explanation: Dense models pay full compute for every parameter on every token. MoE adds many experts per layer but only runs the top-k for a given token, so total capacity (parameters) and per-token compute diverge.

questions.prompt: DeepSeek-V3 activates about 37B of its 671B total parameters per token. Why doesn't this save on GPU memory the way it saves on compute?
options: Because memory and compute are measured in unrelated units that can't be compared
Because serving still requires holding every expert's weights somewhere, since different tokens in a batch can route to different experts
Because DeepSeek-V3 doesn't actually use sparse routing in practice
Because the router itself contains 634B of the model's parameters
questions.explanation: Sparsity is per-token, not per-model. Across a batch, different tokens route to different experts, so all experts' weights must stay loaded (often spread across many GPUs) even though any single token only touches a fraction of them.

questions.prompt: What problem does a load-balancing mechanism (an auxiliary loss, or DeepSeek-V3's bias term) solve during MoE training?
options: It speeds up the router's softmax computation
It prevents the router from collapsing onto a small set of favorite experts while leaving others undertrained
It reduces the total number of parameters in the model
It removes the need for a shared expert
questions.explanation: Without correction, early-popular experts receive more gradient signal and become even more popular, starving the rest. Balancing mechanisms push routing toward underused experts so the whole expert pool stays useful.

posts.title: Hybrid Reasoning Agents: Latent Thought Meets Tool Use
posts.subtitle: One model toggles between silent latent reasoning and transparent text, cutting cost 2.7-3.7x.
posts.summary: HybridAgents reason silently in latent hidden states and switch to text only to call tools or expose their thinking, within a single generation pass. Across 11 agentic benchmarks the authors report a 10.4% average accuracy gain, 35.5-54.7% fewer tokens, and 2.7-3.7x lower cost than frontier agent baselines.

slides.body: Most LLM agents narrate every thought in text. HybridAgents can also think silently in latent space — then switch back to text the instant a tool needs to be called.
slides.title: One Model, Two Ways to Think

bullets: Chain-of-thought agents write out every intermediate thought as tokens — even purely internal ones no tool or human ever reads.
That's expensive: more generated tokens means more latency and more dollars per task, scaling directly with reasoning length.
Purely latent reasoning (no text at all) is efficient but opaque — it can't call tools, and nobody can inspect what the model actually 'thought'.
slides.title: Text-Only Reasoning Is a Tax on Every Thought

bullets: The model runs steps in latent space (dense hidden states, no detokenization) for pure internal reasoning — cheaper per step than generating text tokens.
The instant it needs to call a tool, read a result, or expose a thought for inspection, HybridLink converts the hidden state back into the text embedding space.
A continuous working memory carries the full hybrid history — text, latent thoughts, and tool outputs — across turns, so switching modes never loses context.
slides.body: A lightweight adapter maps the model's last hidden state back into the input embedding space, letting one autoregressive pass move between modes without restarting generation.
slides.title: HybridLink: A Bridge Between Latent and Text

bullets: Stage 1 — HybridSFT: supervised fine-tuning on a Qwen3-14B base teaches the model to generate tool-integrated hybrid sequences at all.
Stage 2 — HybridRL: reinforcement learning then teaches the model WHEN to stay latent versus switch to text — rewarding task success alongside token efficiency.
Latent thoughts can still be decoded into readable pseudo-text on demand, so the efficiency gain doesn't have to come at the total cost of transparency.
slides.title: Two-Stage Training: Teach the Switch, Then Learn When

slides.body: Reported by the authors across 11 agentic benchmarks, versus frontier LLM agents and agentic frameworks.
slides.title: The Numbers: Better Accuracy, Far Fewer Tokens

bullets: Planning which sources to check and how to cross-reference them happens in latent steps — no tokens spent narrating 'I should check source A first.'
The moment it needs to actually issue a search-tool call, HybridLink switches the same forward pass into text mode to emit the structured tool call.
Reading the tool's result and deciding whether to search again can drop back into latent reasoning — only the parts that touch the outside world ever become text.
slides.body: Ask the agent to find a statistic, verify it against two sources, and summarize the result.
slides.title: Worked Example: A Multi-Step Research Task

bullets: Latent reasoning is a learned skill, not a free lunch — it requires the two-stage HybridSFT/HybridRL pipeline; you can't bolt it onto an arbitrary base model with a prompt.
Full auditability takes a hit by default: a latent thought is only human-readable if you explicitly decode it back to pseudo-text, which an always-text baseline never requires.
The efficiency gains compound with reasoning length — short, simple queries that barely reason at all won't see much of the token and cost savings this architecture is built for.
slides.title: Where Latent Reasoning Still Falls Short

bullets: HybridAgents reason in latent hidden states when thinking internally, and switch to text only to call tools or expose reasoning — all within one generation process.
HybridLink is the small adapter that makes that switch possible mid-generation; a continuous working memory keeps context intact across the switches.
Reported gains: +10.4% average accuracy, 35.5-54.7% fewer tokens, 2.7-3.7x lower cost versus frontier agent baselines across 11 benchmarks.
The tradeoff: it needs dedicated two-stage training (HybridSFT + HybridRL), and transparency now requires actively decoding latent thoughts rather than getting them for free.
slides.title: Takeaways

questions.prompt: What problem does HybridLink solve?
options: It compresses text tokens into shorter tokens
It maps the model's hidden state back into the text embedding space, letting one generation pass switch between latent reasoning and text-based tool calls
It replaces the tokenizer with a faster one
It removes the need for any reinforcement learning
questions.explanation: HybridLink is the lightweight adapter that converts a latent hidden state back into the embedding space the model's text/tool-calling path expects, which is what lets a single generation pass move fluidly between silent reasoning and text.

questions.prompt: Why can't a purely latent-reasoning model (no text at all) call external tools on its own?
options: Latent hidden states aren't in the token/embedding space that tool-calling APIs and the model's own text output expect, so there's nothing readable to parse or emit as a tool call
Latent reasoning is always slower than text reasoning
Tools only accept image inputs
Latent models exceed the context window limit
questions.explanation: Tool calls, by definition, have to be expressed as structured text (or similar) that an external system can parse. A model reasoning purely in hidden-state space has no mechanism to produce that without first converting back into the text/embedding space — which is exactly the gap HybridLink bridges.

questions.prompt: What does HybridRL add on top of HybridSFT?
options: A larger vocabulary
The basic ability to generate hybrid sequences at all
Learning WHEN to stay in latent mode versus switch to text, optimizing for both task success and token efficiency — not just the ability to do both
A bigger base model checkpoint
questions.explanation: HybridSFT teaches the model the mechanics of generating tool-integrated hybrid sequences. HybridRL is the second stage that teaches judgment: when staying latent is fine versus when switching to text is necessary, rewarded by both task success and efficiency.

posts.title: Test-Time Compute: Trading Tokens for Accuracy
posts.subtitle: Scaling intelligence by letting a model think longer, not just by training a bigger one.
posts.summary: Test-time compute is a second scaling axis alongside pretraining: spend more inference-time compute — longer reasoning chains, more sampled attempts, or a learned 'think before answering' policy — to get a better answer from the same base model. It pays off most on checkable, multi-step problems like math and code, and far less on open-ended tasks with no single correct answer to converge on.

slides.body: For years, a better model meant a bigger pretraining run. Test-time compute shows you can also get a smarter answer from the SAME model by letting it think longer before responding.
slides.title: A Second Scaling Law: Spend Compute at Inference, Not Just Training

bullets: Each jump in pretrained model capability has required roughly an order-of-magnitude more compute and data — real gains, but an increasingly steep price per point of benchmark improvement.
A single greedy forward pass commits to an answer token-by-token with no ability to backtrack, even on problems that need multi-step deduction.
Many hard problems (competition math, multi-step planning) aren't solved by a bigger model guessing once — they're solved by exploring, checking, and revising.
slides.title: Pretraining Scale Has Diminishing, Expensive Returns

bullets: Chain-of-thought prompting: generate intermediate reasoning tokens before the final answer — the extra tokens are extra compute spent on that one problem.

Self-consistency / majority voting: sample N independent reasoning chains at temperature > 0, take the most common final answer — accuracy rises with N because errors in different chains rarely agree with each other.

Best-of-N with a verifier: generate N candidate solutions, score each with a separate verifier or reward model, keep the highest-scoring one — works well when verifying an answer is easier than producing it.
slides.body: Test-time compute spends extra inference tokens or extra sampled attempts on a single problem, instead of — or in addition to — a bigger model.
slides.title: Let the Model 'Think' Before It Answers

bullets: Rather than relying on prompting alone, reasoning-focused models are trained with reinforcement learning to generate long internal reasoning traces before answering — the 'thinking' is learned, not just prompted.
A process reward model (PRM) can score each intermediate reasoning STEP, not just the final answer, giving a much denser training signal for which reasoning paths to reinforce.
At inference, these models dynamically vary how many 'thinking tokens' they spend per query — simple questions get short traces, hard ones get long ones.
slides.title: How 'Reasoning Models' Bake This In With RL

rows: Multi-step problems a single pass tends to rush
Checking a solution is cheaper than producing it
General reasoning, learned rather than hand-prompted

slides.title: Picking a Test-Time Compute Method

bullets: Greedy single-pass: a model under token pressure can skip a step (forget the 30-minute head start) and confidently output a wrong number.
Chain-of-thought: writing out 'the first train has a 30-mile head start... relative speed is 20mph...' forces the intermediate arithmetic to actually happen as tokens, catching the head-start step.

Self-consistency with 5 samples: if 4 of 5 independent attempts agree on the same final answer despite different reasoning phrasing, that answer is very likely correct — the errors that do occur tend not to repeat identically.
slides.body: 'A train leaves at 2pm going 60mph; another leaves 30 minutes later going 80mph on the same route — when does the second train catch up?'
slides.title: Worked Example: A Multi-Step Word Problem

bullets: Cost scales roughly linearly, or worse, with how much extra compute you spend — self-consistency with N=10 samples means roughly 10x the inference cost for a single query.

It helps most on problems with checkable structure (math, code, logic) where more thinking or more samples converges on a better answer — it does far less for tasks like creative writing or factual recall, where thinking longer doesn't reveal a 'more correct' answer.
Latency rises with reasoning length, which matters for interactive use cases — a model that thinks for 30 seconds isn't a drop-in replacement for a chat response that must return in 1-2 seconds.
Past a point, more samples or longer chains show diminishing returns — self-consistency gains flatten once N is large enough that the majority vote has already stabilized.
slides.title: Test-Time Compute Isn't Free or Universal

bullets: Test-time compute is a second scaling axis alongside pretraining: spend more inference-time compute — longer reasoning, more samples — to get a better answer from the same base model.

Key techniques: chain-of-thought (write out intermediate steps), self-consistency (sample N times, vote), best-of-N with a verifier, and RL-trained reasoning models that learn how much to 'think' per query.
It pays off most on checkable, multi-step problems (math, code, logic) — it's not a universal fix, and cost and latency scale with however much extra compute you spend.

Process reward models that score intermediate reasoning steps, not just final answers, are what let RL training turn 'think longer' into a learned, calibrated behavior rather than a fixed prompting trick.
slides.title: Takeaways

questions.prompt: Why does self-consistency (sampling N reasoning chains and taking the majority answer) tend to improve accuracy?
options: It makes the model's vocabulary larger
Independent sampled reasoning chains tend to make different, uncorrelated errors, so the correct answer — reached via the dominant reasoning path — is more likely to be the majority vote
It automatically fine-tunes the model on the fly
It reduces the number of tokens generated
questions.explanation: Sampling at temperature > 0 produces genuinely different reasoning paths. Correct reasoning tends to converge on the same answer from multiple angles, while mistakes tend to be idiosyncratic to each sample — so the majority vote filters out most individual errors.

questions.prompt: On which kind of task does extra test-time compute (longer reasoning, more samples) help the LEAST?
options: Competition math problems
Multi-step logic puzzles
Open-ended creative writing, where there's no single checkable 'more correct' answer to converge on
Code generation with unit tests
questions.explanation: Test-time compute methods like self-consistency and best-of-N rely on being able to check or vote toward a correct answer. Tasks without a single verifiable right answer don't benefit the same way from 'thinking longer' or sampling more attempts.

questions.prompt: What does a process reward model (PRM) add compared to scoring only the final answer?
options: It scores each intermediate reasoning step, giving a denser training signal for which reasoning paths to reinforce — not just whether the final answer was right
It makes inference faster
It removes the need for any reasoning steps
It only works on math problems
questions.explanation: An outcome reward model only sees pass/fail on the final answer, which is a sparse signal. A process reward model scores each step along the way, letting RL training reinforce good intermediate reasoning even when exploring many different attempts.

posts.title: Context Engineering: Pick the Tokens That Earn Their Place
posts.subtitle: More context isn't more intelligence. It's often just more noise competing for the same attention budget.
posts.summary: Context engineering treats the context window as a scarce resource: curate the smallest set of high-signal tokens for each call instead of dumping everything in. Compaction, structured note-taking, and sub-agents are the three main techniques for outlasting a single window on long-running tasks.

slides.title: Context Engineering: Pick the Tokens That Earn Their Place
slides.body: Prompt engineering asks what to say. Context engineering asks what the model should even be looking at — every system prompt, tool, example, and retrieved fact, chosen fresh on every call.

slides.title: Context Rot Is Real — and It Hits Every Model
bullets: Recall accuracy degrades as token count grows — a documented pattern across model families, not a bug in one of them.
Transformers score pairwise relationships between every token pair, so each token draws against one finite attention budget.
More context isn't free: past a point you're trading signal for noise, not adding capability.

slides.title: The Core Move: Smallest Set of High-Signal Tokens, Chosen Every Call
slides.body: Context engineering extends prompt engineering to everything the model sees, and treats curating it as a per-turn decision, not a one-time setup step.
bullets: System prompts: aim for the 'right altitude' — specific enough to guide behavior, not so hardcoded it breaks on edge cases.
Tools: keep them self-contained and token-efficient in what they return; if a human can't tell which tool applies, the model can't either.
Examples: a handful of diverse, canonical few-shots teaches better than a long list of edge-case rules.

slides.title: Getting Data In: Pre-Loaded Retrieval vs. Just-in-Time
bullets: Pre-inference embedding retrieval front-loads everything the agent might need before it starts reasoning.
Just-in-time retrieval instead gives the agent lightweight pointers — file paths, queries, links — plus tools to pull data on demand.
Claude Code runs a hybrid: it loads CLAUDE.md files upfront, then uses glob, grep, and head/tail to fetch the rest at runtime.
Tradeoff: runtime exploration costs latency and can burn context chasing dead ends; static, well-indexed domains like legal or finance often do better pre-loading instead.

slides.title: Three Techniques for Tasks Longer Than the Window
bullets: Compaction: summarize a nearly-full context and restart from the summary — Claude Code keeps the summary plus the five most recently touched files.

Structured note-taking: the agent writes progress outside the context (a NOTES.md, a to-do list) and reloads it later; Anthropic's memory tool (public beta, shipped with Sonnet 4.5) persists these as files.
Sub-agents: a specialist explores with its own clean context — sometimes tens of thousands of tokens — then hands back a condensed summary of roughly 1,000-2,000 tokens.

slides.title: Which Technique Fits Which Task

rows: Over-compact and you lose precision — tune for recall first
Only as reliable as what the agent chooses to write down
Each one burns tens of thousands of tokens before its ~1-2K summary returns

slides.title: Worked Example: An Agent That Outlasts Its Own Context Window
slides.body: Anthropic's own write-up describes an agent playing a long-running game for thousands of steps — far more than any single context window could hold.
bullets: Every time context nears its limit, the agent writes current state (inventory, map progress, goals) to a notes file instead of trying to keep it all in-window.
On the next turn it reloads only the notes it needs, not the entire multi-thousand-step history.
The same pattern carries over to a long coding session: compact the conversation, keep a running TODO.md, and let sub-agents handle isolated investigations.

slides.title: Where Context Engineering Breaks
bullets: Over-aggressive compaction: summarizing too early or too lossily drops details the agent needed a few turns later.
Tool sprawl: too many overlapping tools, and the model picks the wrong one as often as a confused human would.
Just-in-time retrieval in the wrong domain: chasing files and queries at runtime wastes turns where the data is static and already well-indexed — pre-load there instead.
No universal recipe: as models improve, less manual engineering is needed — start with the simplest approach that works, and add structure only once you've actually hit a limit.

slides.title: Context Engineering, in Four Moves
bullets: Treat the context window as a scarce, curated resource — not a dumping ground for 'just in case' information.
Design tools and examples for clarity first; a model that can't pick the right tool will guess, badly.
Match the technique to the task: compaction for long threads, notes for milestone work, sub-agents for parallel exploration.
Start simple. Add compaction, notes, or sub-agents only once you've actually hit context limits in practice.

questions.prompt: Why does recall accuracy degrade as a conversation's context grows, even with no bugs in the model?
options: The model has a hard token limit that silently truncates old messages
Attention is a finite budget split across pairwise relationships between all tokens, so it stretches thinner as the window fills
Longer contexts always contain more contradictory instructions
The tokenizer compresses old tokens into fewer dimensions
questions.explanation: Transformers compute pairwise attention across every token pair in the context. As token count grows, that same attention budget is spread across more relationships — this 'context rot' shows up across model families, not just one.

questions.prompt: In Claude Code's hybrid retrieval approach, what gets loaded upfront vs. fetched just-in-time?
options: Everything is embedded and retrieved upfront; nothing is fetched at runtime
CLAUDE.md files load upfront; the rest is fetched at runtime via glob, grep, and head/tail
Tool definitions load upfront; CLAUDE.md is fetched on demand
Nothing loads upfront — every file is fetched just-in-time, including CLAUDE.md
questions.explanation: Claude Code pre-loads CLAUDE.md files at the start of a session, then uses lightweight pointers (file paths) and tools like glob/grep/head/tail to pull the rest on demand — a hybrid of pre-loaded and just-in-time retrieval.

questions.prompt: A coding agent has been running for hours and is about to exceed its context window mid-task. Which approach keeps it going without losing critical state?
options: Silently truncate the oldest messages and hope nothing important was in them
Summarize the conversation so far (compaction) and/or persist key state to a notes file it can reload
Switch to a model with a smaller context window
Restart the task from scratch with only the original prompt
questions.explanation: Compaction (summarizing and restarting from the summary) and structured note-taking (writing state to a file like NOTES.md or TODO.md) both let an agent outlast a single context window without discarding what it actually needs.

posts.title: Hybrid Search: Why Vector Search Alone Keeps Missing Exact Matches
posts.subtitle: BM25 catches the needle; embeddings catch the meaning. RRF fuses both.
posts.summary: Dense vector search is great at paraphrase and meaning but routinely buries exact tokens — IDs, error codes, rare names — that a simple keyword index would rank first. Hybrid search runs a lexical index (BM25) and a vector index in parallel, then fuses the two rankings with Reciprocal Rank Fusion so neither failure mode dominates.

slides.title: One Retriever Is Never Enough
slides.body: Dense embeddings and keyword search fail in opposite ways. Hybrid search runs both and combines the rankings instead of picking a winner.

slides.title: Embeddings Blur Exact Tokens Into Meaning
slides.body: A dense embedding packs a whole sentence into one vector optimized for semantic similarity, not character-level recall. Rare, unique strings get averaged away.
bullets: Query 'ERR_CONN_RESET-4432' can rank a doc about 'connection timeout issues' above the one doc that literally contains that exact code.
Product SKUs, part numbers, legal citations, and people's names behave the same way — embeddings cluster them near their topic, not near their exact spelling.
A pure keyword index (BM25) would rank the exact-match document first every time — but it can't find a paraphrased query with zero shared words.

slides.title: Run Both Retrievers, Fuse the Rankings
slides.body: BM25 scores a document by term frequency (saturating, so the 10th occurrence of a word barely counts) divided by document length, with rare terms weighted higher via inverse document frequency. It has no notion of meaning, only exact (or stemmed) token overlap.
bullets: Step 1: send the query to a lexical index (BM25/Elasticsearch) and a vector index (HNSW/IVF) in parallel — same query, two independent ranked lists.
Step 2: fuse with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF): score(doc) = Σ 1 / (k + rank_i) across each list it appears in, where k=60 is the standard default from the original RRF paper.
A doc ranked #1 in BM25 but absent from the vector list still scores 1/61 ≈ 0.016 — high enough to surface, because RRF rewards TOP ranks in ANY list, not average rank.
No score normalization needed — RRF only looks at rank position, so it sidesteps the fact that BM25 and cosine-similarity scores live on totally different scales.

slides.title: The Pipeline: Two Indexes, One Fused List
slides.body: Both retrievers run concurrently, not in sequence — hybrid search adds a parallel branch, not a slower chain.
bullets: Query → BM25 index → top-K lexical candidates (e.g. K=100)
Query → embedding model → vector index → top-K semantic candidates (K=100)
Both candidate lists → RRF fusion → single ranked list → (optional) cross-encoder reranker on the top ~20 → final context for the LLM.
Each index is maintained independently, so a doc update means writing to both — that's the operational cost you're paying for the recall gain.

slides.title: Where Each Approach Wins
Worked Example: The Error Code That Vector Search Lost
slides.body: A support-ticket search for "ERR_CONN_RESET-4432 keeps happening after deploy" against 50k internal docs.
bullets: Vector-only: top result is a generic 'troubleshooting connection timeouts' guide — close in meaning, wrong doc. The exact-match runbook ranks #14, likely never seen.
BM25-only: the runbook containing 'ERR_CONN_RESET-4432' ranks #1 on exact token match, but a differently-worded query like 'socket keeps dropping after release' would miss it entirely.

Hybrid + RRF: the runbook is #1 in BM25 (score contribution 1/61) and still appears somewhere in the vector list (say rank 8, contributing 1/68) — its combined RRF score beats documents that only appear in one list, so it surfaces at #1 either way the question is phrased.

slides.title: When Hybrid Search Isn't Worth It
slides.body: Hybrid search is a real engineering cost, not a free upgrade — add it only when the failure mode it fixes is actually present in your corpus.
bullets: Small corpora (a few thousand docs): a single reranker pass over the full set is often cheaper and just as accurate as maintaining two indexes.
Pure-paraphrase workloads with no IDs, codes, or jargon (e.g. casual chat search) gain little from BM25 and just add latency and ops overhead.
The fusion constant k and per-list top-K still need tuning per corpus — the RRF defaults aren't universal, and skipping that tuning silently caps your recall gains.
Two indexes mean two things to keep in sync; a doc deleted from one and not the other produces ghost hits or silent gaps.

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Vector search and keyword search fail in opposite, complementary ways — exact tokens vs. paraphrased meaning.
Reciprocal Rank Fusion (score = Σ 1/(k+rank), k≈60) combines ranked lists without needing to normalize incompatible similarity scores.
Hybrid search is two indexes running in parallel, not a slower sequential pipeline — the cost is operational (sync, tuning), not latency.
Add a cross-encoder reranker on the fused top-K for the final precision boost most production RAG systems use.

questions.prompt: A user searches for an exact error code like 'ERR_CONN_RESET-4432'. Why might a pure vector (embedding) search fail to surface the one document containing that exact string?
options: Vector search only works on documents shorter than 100 words
Embeddings compress text toward semantic meaning, so an exact rare token can be outweighed by overall topical similarity to other documents
Vector indexes cannot store numbers or symbols
Vector search always returns documents in alphabetical order
questions.explanation: Embeddings are trained to cluster by meaning, not exact spelling. A document that's merely topically close (e.g., 'connection timeouts') can out-rank the one literal match because the embedding doesn't specially weight rare exact tokens — that's precisely what a lexical index like BM25 is good at.

questions.prompt: In Reciprocal Rank Fusion, a document's score from one ranked list is 1/(k + rank). Why use rank position instead of the retriever's raw similarity score?
options: Rank-based fusion is always faster to compute than score-based fusion
BM25 scores and cosine-similarity scores live on different, incompatible scales, so combining raw scores directly would be meaningless without careful normalization — rank position sidesteps that
Raw scores are not available from vector databases
Using ranks guarantees the top result is always correct
questions.explanation: BM25 scores can range widely and unboundedly based on term statistics, while cosine similarity is bounded between -1 and 1. Averaging or summing them directly would let whichever retriever has a bigger numeric range dominate. RRF avoids this entirely by only using each document's rank position within its own list.

questions.prompt: When is hybrid search LEAST likely to be worth its added complexity?
options: When the corpus is large and full of product IDs, error codes, and jargon
When queries are a mix of exact lookups and paraphrased questions
When the corpus is small (a few thousand docs) with no exact-match identifiers, so a single reranker pass over all candidates is already fast and accurate
When latency budgets are generous
questions.explanation: Hybrid search earns its keep when exact-match tokens exist AND the corpus is large enough that you can't just rerank everything. For a small corpus with no IDs or jargon, the two-index operational overhead (sync, tuning, infra) usually isn't worth the marginal recall gain.

posts.title: HNSW: How Vector Search Skips Checking Everything
posts.subtitle: A layered graph of shortcuts turns a billion-item search into a few dozen hops
posts.summary: HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) is the graph structure behind most vector database nearest-neighbor search: it builds several layers of a proximity graph, sparse long-range links on top and dense short-range links at the bottom, so a query can greedily hop toward its nearest neighbors in roughly logarithmic time instead of scanning every vector. It trades a small, tunable chance of missing the true nearest neighbor for orders-of-magnitude faster search, at the cost of extra memory for the graph and messier deletes.

slides.title: Your RAG pipeline never actually checks every vector
slides.body: When a vector database answers a similarity query over tens of millions of embeddings in a few milliseconds, it isn't comparing the query against every single one. It's walking a graph.
bullets: Exact nearest-neighbor search is linear in the number of vectors — too slow past a few hundred thousand
HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) is the graph index most vector DBs use instead
It's approximate: it can miss the single best match in exchange for huge speedups

slides.title: Brute-force kNN scales with every vector you add
slides.body: Comparing a query embedding against N stored vectors costs O(N x d) — d is the embedding dimension. Double your corpus, double every query's latency. There's no shortcut without changing the data structure.
bullets: A 768-dim embedding search over 10M vectors means 7.68 billion multiply-adds per query, brute force
Latency grows linearly with corpus size — fine at 10K rows, unworkable at 100M
Adding a GPU helps the constant factor, not the underlying linear scaling

slides.title: Build a graph where greedy hops lead toward the answer
slides.body: HNSW inserts every vector as a node and wires it to its approximate nearest neighbors, forming several stacked layers. The top layer is sparse with long-range links; each layer below is denser, and the bottom layer contains every node with only short-range, local links — a classic 'small world' structure.
bullets: Search starts at an entry point in the top layer and greedily moves to whichever neighbor is closer to the query
When no neighbor at the current layer is closer, the search drops down one layer and keeps greedily hopping
By the bottom layer, the search is already near the true neighborhood, so only a small local candidate list needs checking
Parameter M caps links per node; higher M means better recall but a bigger graph

slides.title: HNSW vs. the other common index choices
slides.body: Relative shape of the tradeoffs, not figures from any specific benchmark — actual numbers depend heavily on dataset, dimension, and tuning.

rows: Highest — graph edges on top of vectors

slides.title: Worked example: searching 1 million product embeddings
slides.body: Say a catalog has 1M product embeddings indexed with HNSW using M=16 (max 16 links per node) and ef_construction=200 (candidate list size while building). A query arrives with ef_search=50.
bullets: The search enters at the top layer's single entry point and greedily walks toward the query — maybe 4-5 hops across a handful of sparse layers
At the bottom layer it maintains a candidate list of up to ef_search=50 nodes, expanding outward from the current best
Total distance computations end up in the hundreds, not the full 1,000,000 — because the graph already pruned almost everywhere irrelevant
Raising ef_search to 200 checks more candidates, trading some latency for a few extra points of recall

slides.title: Where HNSW pays off — and where it bites you
slides.body: HNSW is the default in Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, Milvus, and pgvector's hnsw index type for good reason, but it isn't free.
bullets: Graph edges add real memory on top of the raw vectors — often 1.5-2x the vector data size, which matters at hundreds of millions of rows
Deletes aren't native: most implementations mark nodes as tombstones and periodically rebuild rather than truly removing them, so delete-heavy workloads degrade the graph over time
Build time is nontrivial — inserting a vector means searching the graph as it exists so far, so index construction itself is sequential-ish work, not a cheap bulk load
For a small, mostly-static corpus (a few thousand to low tens of thousands of vectors), brute-force flat search can be just as fast and far simpler to reason about — skip HNSW there
Filtered search (e.g. 'nearest neighbors where category = X') isn't natively graph-aware, so heavily filtered queries can force the search to explore far more of the graph than usual

slides.title: The core idea in one line
slides.body: HNSW turns 'is this vector close to my query?' from a question you ask N times into a question you ask a few dozen times, by pre-building shortcuts that route a greedy walk straight into the right neighborhood.
bullets: Sparse long links on top get you across the space fast; dense short links at the bottom get you precise
Recall vs. speed is a dial (ef_search), not a fixed property of the index
It's approximate by design — the right trade when 'almost certainly the nearest neighbors, instantly' beats 'guaranteed exact, eventually'

questions.prompt: Why can HNSW answer a nearest-neighbor query without comparing it to every stored vector?
options: It pre-computes and caches the answer to every possible query
It compresses all vectors into a single average vector
It walks a multi-layer graph greedily, using sparse long-range links to jump close fast and dense local links to refine, checking only a small candidate set
It randomly samples a subset of vectors each time and hopes one is close
questions.explanation: HNSW's layered proximity graph lets a query greedily hop toward its neighborhood, layer by layer, so only the nodes actually visited along the way and their close neighbors get checked — not the whole dataset.

questions.prompt: What does raising the ef_search parameter trade for higher recall?
options: Nothing — it's strictly free
More query latency, since a larger candidate list gets explored and compared
Less memory usage
It only affects index build time, not search
questions.explanation: ef_search controls how large a candidate list the search maintains while exploring the graph. A bigger list means more distance computations per query — slower, but more likely to find the true nearest neighbors.

questions.prompt: When is plain brute-force (flat) search often the better choice over HNSW?
options: Any time the corpus exceeds 1,000 vectors
Never — HNSW always wins
When the corpus is small and mostly static, where brute force is simple, exact, and already fast enough
Only when running on a GPU
questions.explanation: HNSW's graph overhead (memory, build time, tombstone-based deletes) only pays off once brute-force scanning is actually too slow. For small or rarely-changing collections, exact flat search is simpler and the performance gap barely matters.

posts.title: Multi-Head Latent Attention: Shrinking the Cache That Eats Your GPU
posts.subtitle: Compress keys and values into one latent vector, decompress per head at attention time
posts.summary: Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) compresses the keys and values every attention head would normally cache into one small shared latent vector, then reconstructs full per-head keys and values on the fly with learned projections. It shrinks the KV cache far more than grouping heads (GQA/MQA) without averaging away per-head expressiveness, at the cost of extra matmuls and a split-out rotary component.

slides.title: The KV cache, not the weights, is what runs out of memory
slides.body: Every token an LLM generates adds a key and value vector to a running cache for every attention head, in every layer. At long context lengths that cache can outgrow the model's own weights in GPU memory.
bullets: Long-context serving is bottlenecked by cache size, not FLOPs
MLA compresses that cache into a shared latent per token
First shipped in DeepSeek-V2, then DeepSeek-V3

slides.title: Standard multi-head attention caches one K and V per head, per layer, per token
slides.body: In vanilla multi-head attention (MHA), each of the H heads has its own key and value vector of size d_head. The KV cache per token per layer is 2 x H x d_head numbers (the 2 is for K and V) — and you pay that for every layer and every token you've generated so far.
bullets: Cache size scales linearly with sequence length, heads, and layers
Doubling context length doubles the cache; it does not touch the weights
More concurrent requests means more caches live in memory at once, which caps batch size

slides.title: MQA and GQA cut the cache by sharing; MLA cuts it by compressing
slides.body: Multi-Query Attention (MQA) gives every head the same single K/V pair — cheapest cache, but heads lose their distinct 'view' of the sequence. Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) is a middle ground: a few shared K/V groups split across heads. MLA takes a different path: project each token's K and V down into one small shared latent vector, cache only that latent, and reconstruct full per-head K and V from it with a learned up-projection matrix at attention time.
bullets: The latent is low-rank: far fewer dimensions than H x d_head
Up-projection matrices are learned per-head, so heads stay distinct — nothing is literally shared/copied like in GQA
Rotary position embeddings (RoPE) don't survive this compression cleanly, so MLA splits off a small decoupled RoPE slice that bypasses compression and is cached separately, uncompressed

slides.title: Cache footprint per token, same head count and head dimension
slides.body: Relative KV cache size per token per layer for H heads of dimension d_head, compared to plain MHA (2 x H x d_head). Figures are illustrative of the mechanism's shape, not a benchmark from any specific paper.

rows: Full K, V for every head
One shared K, V for all heads
None — all heads read identical K/V
Partial — heads in a group are identical
One low-rank latent vector + small RoPE slice
Smaller than GQA at similar group counts
Full — each head gets its own learned reconstruction

slides.title: Worked example: 8 heads, 64 dims each, one layer, one token
slides.body: Take H=8 heads with d_head=64. MHA caches 2 x 8 x 64 = 1024 numbers for that token in that layer. A GQA setup with 2 groups caches 2 x 2 x 64 = 256 numbers, but now 4 heads in each group see the exact same K and V — they've lost their individual perspective. MLA instead caches a single compressed latent of, say, 256-512 numbers (a hyperparameter, not tied to head count) plus a small decoupled RoPE slice. At inference, 8 separate learned matrices expand that one latent back into 8 distinct per-head K/V pairs — so you get GQA-like cache savings without GQA's head-collapsing.
bullets: Compression ratio is a design knob (latent size), not fixed by head count like GQA
The up-projection weights are learned during pretraining, not bolted on after
Decompression adds a matmul per attention call — a compute-for-memory trade

slides.title: When this trade is worth making — and when it isn't
slides.body: MLA pays off hardest exactly where KV cache dominates: very long context, high concurrency serving. It pays off least where cache was never the bottleneck.
bullets: Don't bolt MLA onto an already-trained MHA model — the up/down-projection matrices need to be learned jointly with the rest of the network during pretraining, so retrofitting it post-hoc throws away that benefit
The decoupled RoPE path adds real implementation and kernel complexity versus plain GQA — only worth it once cache savings matter
On short-context, low-concurrency workloads (a single long-running chat, a small on-device model) the extra decompression matmuls can cost more than the cache savings buy back
Needs a fused, optimized kernel to realize its speed advantage — a naive implementation can be slower than GQA despite the smaller cache

slides.title: The core idea in one line
slides.body: MLA bets that a token's keys and values across all heads share most of their information — so store that shared signal once, in compressed form, and let cheap per-head matrices recover what each head actually needs at attention time.
bullets: GQA shrinks the cache by making heads share identical values
MLA shrinks the cache by finding a smaller representation that still lets every head differ
The latent dimension is tunable, decoupling cache size from head count entirely

questions.prompt: What does Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) actually store in the KV cache?
options: A full key and value vector for every attention head
One shared key/value pair reused by all heads
A single compressed low-rank latent vector (plus a small decoupled RoPE slice), later expanded per head
Nothing — it recomputes keys and values from scratch at every step
questions.explanation: MLA caches a compressed latent representation of K/V, not the full per-head vectors (MHA) or a single shared pair (MQA). Per-head keys and values are reconstructed from that latent using learned up-projection matrices when attention is computed.

questions.prompt: Why does MLA split out a separate, uncompressed path for rotary position embeddings (RoPE)?
options: RoPE is only needed during training, not inference
RoPE's rotation makes the key space harder to compress losslessly through a shared low-rank projection, so it's kept outside the compressed latent
RoPE requires more memory than the rest of the key vector combined
It's a historical artifact with no technical reason
questions.explanation: Applying RoPE's position-dependent rotation before compressing keys into a shared latent interferes with the low-rank structure MLA relies on, so MLA decouples a small RoPE-carrying slice of the key vector and caches it separately, uncompressed.

questions.prompt: In which scenario does MLA's cache savings matter least?
options: Serving many concurrent users with 100K+ token contexts
A single short chat session on a small model where memory was never the bottleneck
A high-throughput inference cluster running at max batch size
A long-document summarization service
questions.explanation: MLA trades extra decompression compute for a smaller cache. When context is short and concurrency is low, the cache was never the constraint, so that compute trade can be a net loss rather than a win.

posts.title: WeVisOne-VL: One Model for Boxes, Masks, and Mattes
posts.subtitle: Tencent swaps SAM for a 9.6M-parameter decoder bolted onto a single <OBJ> token.
posts.summary: WeVisOne-VL unifies detection, counting, OCR, segmentation, and matting into one vision-language model by adding a tiny pixel decoder behind a single <OBJ> token, trained on a knowledge-graph-driven data engine that labeled over 100M images.

slides.title: A VLM That Also Segments, Mattes, and Says 'Not There'
slides.body: Tencent's WeChat Vision team released WeVisOne-VL-2B and -4B, open weights built on Qwen3-VL, Apache-2.0.
bullets: Unifies 6 vision tasks: detection, referring, counting, OCR, segmentation, matting
Built on Qwen3-VL — adds a small pixel decoder, not a second foundation model
Released Oct 22, 2026 as open weights at huggingface.co/tencent

slides.title: Pixel-Level Vision Used to Mean Stacking 4 Separate Models
slides.body: A typical pipeline chains a detector, SAM for masks, a separate matting network, and an OCR model — each handoff loses information and adds a failure point.
bullets: Detector finds boxes, SAM turns boxes into masks, a third model does alpha matting, a fourth reads text
Every handoff between models is a place errors compound and latency stacks up
None of those models can say 'that object isn't in the image' — they just output their best (wrong) guess

slides.title: One <OBJ> Token Drives a 9.6M-Parameter Pixel Decoder
slides.body: The VLM predicts a box using coordinate tokens <0>-<1000>, then emits an <OBJ> token whose hidden state — plus the box and multi-level Qwen3-VL ViT features — feeds a tiny decoder that outputs a full-resolution mask or alpha matte.
bullets: No SAM call required: the decoder is 9.6M params, bolted directly onto the VLM's own features
Same token-prediction interface handles boxes, points, counts, OCR text, masks, and mattes
When nothing matches the query, the model outputs None instead of hallucinating a box

slides.title: 100M+ Images, Labeled by a Knowledge Graph, Not Just Humans
slides.body: A knowledge-graph-driven pipeline discovers concepts, localizes them with expert models, and has a VLM verify the result before boxes are extended into masks and alpha mattes.
bullets: Expert models propose candidates; a VLM filters/verifies before anything is kept
Verified boxes are auto-extended to segmentation masks and matting alpha channels
The matting annotator (Mask2Alpha) is released separately on a dedicated branch

slides.title: The 4B Model Beats the Best Open Baseline on Every Task Tested
slides.body: Numbers from the project's own benchmark table (best open baseline vs. WeVisOne-VL-4B):
bullets: Rejection rate (WeRef-Bench) jumps from 73.0% to 96.4% — the biggest single gain
Matting error (P3M-500-NP, lower is better) drops from 15.4 to 7.3 MAD

slides.title: Worked Example: Finding Text in a Cluttered Photo, or Nothing
slides.body: Query the model with 'find the word SALE' on a storefront photo and it returns boxes plus the exact text. Query it for 'the red backpack' on a photo with no backpack, and the WeRef-Bench-trained rejection head answers None instead of pointing at the nearest red object.
bullets: OCR + grounding in one call: locate text, read it, and box it — no separate OCR model
The None output matters in production: a hallucinated box on an absent object is worse than no answer at all

slides.title: Where It Falls Short
slides.body: The pixel decoder is tiny, but it still rides on a 2B or 4B backbone — far from edge-device territory, and the README ships fine-tuning code as a TODO, not a feature.
bullets: 2B/4B VLM backbone means this isn't a drop-in for phone-sized or embedded deployments
Training data comes from an automated knowledge-graph pipeline verified by another VLM — it inherits whatever biases that verifier has
No official fine-tuning recipe yet, so adapting it to a narrow domain means waiting or reverse-engineering the training code

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: A single <OBJ> token plus a 9.6M-param decoder replaces a 4-model vision pipeline
Explicit None rejection (96.4% on WeRef-Bench) beats forcing a guess on absent objects
Open Apache-2.0 weights at 2B/4B, built on Qwen3-VL, with code and demo on GitHub/Hugging Face

questions.prompt: What does WeVisOne-VL's <OBJ> token actually trigger?
options: A 9.6M-parameter pixel decoder that turns the token's hidden state + box + ViT features into a mask or matte
The end of the generated sentence
A separate SAM call for segmentation
A resize of the input image
questions.explanation: The <OBJ> token's hidden state, combined with its predicted box and multi-level Qwen3-VL ViT features, is exactly what the pixel decoder consumes to produce a full-resolution mask or alpha matte — no SAM involved.

questions.prompt: On WeRef-Bench, the baseline's rejection rate was 73.0%. What does 'rejection rate' measure here?
options: How often the model correctly outputs None when the queried object isn't in the image
How often the model's answer is rejected by a human reviewer
The model's refusal rate on unsafe prompts
How many training images were rejected by the data pipeline
questions.explanation: Rejection rate is about trustworthiness, not safety: a model asked to find something absent from the image should say so (None) instead of hallucinating a box. WeVisOne-VL-4B pushes this from 73.0% to 96.4%.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't WeVisOne-VL need a separate SAM model for segmentation?
options: Its own 9.6M-param pixel decoder, fed by the VLM's existing ViT features, generates masks directly
Segmentation isn't actually supported
It calls SAM internally but hides the API
Masks are computed with classical edge detection, not a model
questions.explanation: The pixel decoder reuses features the VLM already computed (multi-level Qwen3-VL ViT features) instead of routing through an external segmentation model like SAM — that's the core efficiency claim.

posts.title: Claude Sonnet 5.5: Faster and Cheaper, Not Weaker

slides.title: The Mid-Tier Model Just Jumped the Line
slides.body: Released September 28, 2026 as the second model in the Claude 5.5 family, after Opus 5.5.
bullets: 30%+ faster output than Sonnet 5, up to 30% lower cost per task

First Sonnet model to beat Pokémon Red using only screenshots

slides.body: Frontier benchmarks get the headlines, but most production traffic runs on the mid-tier model — so a speed or cost change there compounds across millions of calls in a way a flagship upgrade never touches.
bullets: Sonnet, not Opus, is usually the default model wired into agents and IDE tools
A 30% cost cut per task is a 30% cut on your entire fleet's bill, not one benchmark run

First Sonnet model with distillation-resistant safety classifiers; expanded preserved-thinking ties reasoning to the originating account

posts.title: KV Cache: Why LLMs Don't Recompute Every Token
posts.subtitle: The memory trade that makes fast chat replies possible — and expensive at long context.
posts.summary: Every generated token needs attention scores against every prior token. The KV cache stores each layer's Key/Value projections once so decoding only computes the new token's attention — trading GPU memory for avoiding O(n²) repeated work, until that memory becomes the real bottleneck.

slides.title: The Hidden Memory Tax Behind Every Chat Reply
slides.body: Without a KV cache, generating token N means recomputing attention over all N-1 previous tokens from scratch — at every layer, for every token you've already generated.
bullets: A KV cache stores each layer's Key and Value projections once they're computed
Each new token only computes attention against what's stored — not the whole conversation again

slides.title: Without Caching, Generation Redoes Work It Already Paid For
slides.body: Attention needs a Key and Value vector for every previous token, at every layer, to score against the current token's Query. Recomputing all of them on every step wastes compute that produced the identical result a moment ago.
bullets: Token 500 would recompute K/V for tokens 1-499 all over again, at every one of the model's layers
That's pure waste: those K/V vectors for past tokens never change once computed

slides.title: Compute Once, Append, Attend — Per Layer, Per Step
slides.body: At each decoding step the model computes Query/Key/Value only for the new token, appends that token's K and V to a running per-layer cache, then attends the new Query against everything stored so far.
bullets: Cache shape per layer: [batch, num_kv_heads, sequence_length, head_dim] for K and for V
The Query for the new token is the only fresh computation that touches the full history

slides.title: Worked Math: How Big Does This Get?
slides.body: For a 7B-class model with 32 layers, 32 KV heads, head dim 128, stored in fp16 (2 bytes): one token costs 2 (K and V) × 32 layers × 32 heads × 128 dims × 2 bytes ≈ 512KB. At an 8K-token context, that's roughly 4GB — per sequence, before the model's own weights.
bullets: 512KB/token × 8,192 tokens ≈ 4GB of cache for a single 8K-context conversation
Double the context, double the cache — it scales linearly with sequence length and with batch size

slides.title: Fewer KV Heads Shrinks the Cache Directly
slides.body: Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) keeps many query heads but shares Key/Value projections across groups of them — cutting cache size by exactly the head-sharing ratio. Llama 2 70B is a real example: 64 query heads, grouped down to 8 KV heads.
bullets: This is why GQA and KV-cache quantization (fp16 → int8/int4) matter more at long context than at short context
PagedAttention (used by vLLM) attacks the same budget from a different angle: less fragmentation, not fewer bytes per token

slides.title: Why Your Batch Size Caps Out Before Your GPU Does
slides.body: Say a GPU has 24GB free after loading model weights, and each 8K-context conversation needs ~4GB of KV cache on an MHA model. You can fit roughly 6 concurrent conversations — not because the GPU ran out of FLOPs, but because the cache ran out of memory first.
bullets: Swap to a GQA model with 1/8th the cache and the same GPU now fits far more concurrent sequences at the same context length
This is the actual mechanism behind 'continuous batching' needing a tight memory budget to pack requests efficiently

slides.title: Where the Cache Becomes the Problem
slides.body: The KV cache is a straight trade: skip recomputation, pay in memory that grows without bound as conversations get longer or more concurrent.
bullets: At long context or high concurrency, KV cache can dwarf the model weights' own memory footprint
Quantizing the cache (int8/int4) saves memory but adds a small, measurable accuracy cost — it's not free
The cache for one request generally can't be reused by an unrelated one, though shared prompt prefixes across requests can share cached K/V (the mechanism behind prompt caching)

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: KV cache trades recomputation for memory: compute each token's K/V once, reuse it for every future step
Cache size scales linearly with context length × batch size — it's often the real limit on concurrency, not FLOPs
GQA, KV-cache quantization, and PagedAttention are three different levers on the same memory budget

questions.prompt: What exactly does the KV cache store?
options: The Key and Value projections computed for every previous token, at every layer
The full hidden state of the model at every layer
Only the final attention output for each token
The model's gradients during training
questions.explanation: Attention needs K and V vectors for every prior token at every layer to score against new Queries. The KV cache stores exactly those K/V projections once, so they never need recomputing.

questions.prompt: Why does Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) shrink the KV cache compared to standard multi-head attention (MHA)?
options: It shares Key/Value projections across groups of query heads, so fewer distinct K/V vectors are cached — e.g. Llama 2 70B caches only 8 KV heads instead of 64
It deletes the cache after a fixed number of tokens
It stores K/V in a different data type automatically
It skips caching for the first half of the conversation
questions.explanation: GQA keeps many query heads for expressiveness but groups them to share far fewer Key/Value heads — Llama 2 70B goes from 64 query heads down to 8 KV heads, an 8x cache reduction, with no change to how many tokens are stored.

questions.prompt: In the worked example, why does a GPU's usable batch size cap out at a handful of concurrent long-context conversations even though it has plenty of compute left?
options: The KV cache's memory footprint (linear in context length × batch size) fills the GPU's memory before compute becomes the bottleneck
The model can only process one conversation at a time
Long contexts are rejected by the attention mechanism above a hard limit
GPUs can't run more than 6 processes simultaneously
questions.explanation: Each additional concurrent sequence adds its own KV cache (here, ~4GB per 8K-context MHA conversation). Memory for the cache runs out well before the GPU's FLOPs are saturated, which is exactly why techniques that shrink the cache (GQA, quantization) let you serve more concurrent users on the same hardware.
